prompt: Why is internal fertilization common on land while external fertilization is common in water?
correct: Internal fertilization protects gametes/zygotes from drying and does not require surrounding water, but requires mating and fewer gametes may be produced. External fertilization can release many gametes and works well in water, but is vulnerable to dilution/predation and desiccation on land.
correctWhy: Internal fertilization protects gametes/zygotes from drying and does not require surrounding water, but requires mating and fewer gametes may be produced. External fertilization can release many gametes and works well in water, but is vulnerable to dilution/predation and desiccation on land.

close.text: Internal fertilization protects gametes from desiccation on land, while external fertilization works well in water where gametes can meet; however, external fertilization is usually more reliable on dry land because gametes spread farther through air.
close.whyWrong: Unprotected gametes desiccate rapidly on land; water facilitates external fertilization.

close.text: Internal fertilization reduces dependence on environmental water, but it is common on land only because terrestrial animals produce more gametes than aquatic external fertilizers.
close.whyWrong: External fertilization often involves very large numbers of gametes; internal fertilization can use fewer with greater protection.

medium.text: Internal and external fertilization differ only in embryo color.
medium.whyWrong: They differ in where gametes meet and their environmental requirements.

medium.text: External fertilization means eggs are fertilized inside the female, while internal fertilization happens in open water.
medium.whyWrong: The terms are reversed.

clear.text: Water prevents sperm from swimming, so external fertilization is impossible in aquatic animals.
clear.whyWrong: Water is the medium that allows many externally released gametes to survive and meet.

clear.text: Land animals use internal fertilization because they lack gametes.
clear.whyWrong: They still produce gametes; fertilization occurs inside the reproductive tract.

prompt: What advantages do reptile/amniote eggs have over amphibian eggs?
correct: Amniote eggs resist desiccation, contain protective/nutrient/exchange membranes, and can develop on land; typical amphibian eggs lack a water-resistant shell and are usually tied to aquatic/moist environments.
correctWhy: Amniote eggs resist desiccation, contain protective/nutrient/exchange membranes, and can develop on land; typical amphibian eggs lack a water-resistant shell and are usually tied to aquatic/moist environments.

close.text: Amniote eggs resist desiccation and contain membranes for protection, nutrition, waste, and gas exchange, but amphibian eggs have an even more water-resistant shell and therefore are less tied to moist environments.
close.whyWrong: Typical amphibian eggs lack the desiccation-resistant amniotic shell and remain water/moisture dependent.

close.text: Reptile/amniote eggs can develop on land, but the advantage comes mainly from making the embryo completely isolated from oxygen exchange.
close.whyWrong: Gas exchange must continue; the shell/membranes balance exchange with water conservation.

medium.text: Amniote eggs contain no extraembryonic membranes and therefore require more standing water than amphibian eggs.
medium.whyWrong: Extraembryonic membranes are central to their terrestrial advantage.

medium.text: Amphibian and amniote eggs are identical in shell and water dependence.
medium.whyWrong: Their differences are a major vertebrate evolutionary transition.

clear.text: Amniote eggs are adapted only for ocean life.
clear.whyWrong: They helped free reproduction from standing water on land.

clear.text: The shell's purpose is to prevent any gas from entering or leaving.
clear.whyWrong: Gas exchange is essential and occurs through the shell/membranes.

prompt: Distinguish the major living reptile clades and their defining traits.
correct: Testudines: turtles with shells. Squamata: lizards/snakes with kinetic skulls. Crocodilia: crocodilians with four-chambered heart, socketed teeth, parental care. Aves: birds, dinosaur-derived reptiles with feathers and flight adaptations. Tuataras represent another small living reptile lineage.
correctWhy: Testudines: turtles with shells. Squamata: lizards/snakes with kinetic skulls. Crocodilia: crocodilians with four-chambered heart, socketed teeth, parental care. Aves: birds, dinosaur-derived reptiles with feathers and flight adaptations. Tuataras represent another small living reptile lineage.

close.text: Turtles are Testudines, lizards/snakes Squamata, crocodilians Crocodilia, birds Aves, and tuataras a small separate lineage; however, birds are excluded from reptiles because feathers erase their dinosaur ancestry.
close.whyWrong: Modern phylogeny places birds within reptiles/dinosaurs.

close.text: Crocodilians have socketed teeth, parental care, and a four-chambered heart, but squamates—not birds—are the dinosaur-derived feathered lineage.
close.whyWrong: Birds are the dinosaur-derived reptile lineage.

medium.text: Testudines are frogs, Squamata are sharks, Crocodilia are mammals, and Aves are insects.
medium.whyWrong: These are incorrect identifications of reptile clades.

medium.text: All living reptiles belong to one clade with identical skulls, hearts, and integument, so there is no meaningful subdivision.
medium.whyWrong: Living reptiles contain several distinctive lineages.

clear.text: Birds are not vertebrates.
clear.whyWrong: Birds are vertebrate reptiles.

clear.text: Turtles are mollusks because they have shells.
clear.whyWrong: Turtles are reptiles; shells evolved independently from molluscan shells.

prompt: How did vertebrate circulation evolve from two-chambered to four-chambered hearts, and why does it matter?
correct: Fishes use a two-chambered heart and single circuit. Amphibians and most reptiles use double circulation with incomplete ventricular separation and some mixing. Crocodilians, birds, and mammals have four chambers and complete separation, supporting efficient high-pressure systemic flow and high metabolism.
correctWhy: Fishes use a two-chambered heart and single circuit. Amphibians and most reptiles use double circulation with incomplete ventricular separation and some mixing. Crocodilians, birds, and mammals have four chambers and complete separation, supporting efficient high-pressure systemic flow and high metabolism.

close.text: Vertebrate circulation became progressively more separated as pulmonary and systemic circuits evolved: fishes use two chambers, amphibians/reptiles have partial separation, and birds/mammals have four chambers. The advantage of four chambers is that they lower systemic pressure and deliberately mix the two blood streams to conserve energy.
close.whyWrong: The chamber sequence is broadly right, but the functional conclusion is reversed. Four chambers keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate and support efficient high-pressure systemic delivery and high metabolism.

close.text: Four-chambered hearts separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, but fish already use a four-chambered double circulation identical to mammals.
close.whyWrong: Fish typically have a two-chambered heart and single circuit.

medium.text: Heart evolution progressed from four chambers in fish to two chambers in mammals because land animals need less oxygen.
medium.whyWrong: The broad trend is toward greater separation, culminating in four chambers in birds/mammals/crocodilians.

medium.text: The number of heart chambers affects only body color, not blood flow or oxygen delivery.
medium.whyWrong: Separation and circuit pressure strongly affect circulatory efficiency.

clear.text: All vertebrates have identical hearts.
clear.whyWrong: Major structural differences occur among fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.

clear.text: Four-chambered hearts mix oxygenated and deoxygenated blood more than three-chambered hearts.
clear.whyWrong: They provide more complete separation.

prompt: How do amphibians reduce problems caused by mixing blood in one ventricle?
correct: They can regulate flow patterns through the heart and use pulmonary/skin respiration; anatomical ridges and timing reduce complete mixing even without a fully divided ventricle.
correctWhy: They can regulate flow patterns through the heart and use pulmonary/skin respiration; anatomical ridges and timing reduce complete mixing even without a fully divided ventricle.

close.text: Amphibians can direct blood flow using timing and internal ridges and also exchange gases through lungs/skin, but their single ventricle mixes oxygenated and deoxygenated blood completely with no flow separation at all.
close.whyWrong: Mixing is incomplete; anatomy and flow dynamics reduce it.

close.text: Flow regulation helps amphibians manage a three-chambered heart, but they solve mixing primarily by closing the lungs and sending all blood through one undivided vessel.
close.whyWrong: Pulmonary/skin circuits and intracardiac flow patterns help manage separation; shutting lungs is not the general solution.

medium.text: Amphibians avoid mixing by having a fully four-chambered heart like birds.
medium.whyWrong: Typical amphibians have two atria and one ventricle.

medium.text: They reduce mixing by eliminating red blood cells.
medium.whyWrong: Red blood cells are essential for oxygen transport and are not eliminated.

clear.text: Mixing is not an issue because amphibians never transport oxygen in blood.
clear.whyWrong: Blood transport is important alongside cutaneous/pulmonary respiration.

clear.text: The single ventricle is divided by an exoskeleton.
clear.whyWrong: Flow control involves internal cardiac anatomy and timing, not an exoskeleton.

prompt: What evidence shows that birds are reptiles, and what four bird features support flight?
correct: Fossils such as Archaeopteryx combine dinosaur and bird traits; morphology and molecular phylogenies nest birds within dinosaurs/reptiles. Flight features: feathers, efficient air-sac respiration, reduced organs/body mass, and lightweight hollow/honeycombed bones.
correctWhy: Fossils such as Archaeopteryx combine dinosaur and bird traits; morphology and molecular phylogenies nest birds within dinosaurs/reptiles. Flight features: feathers, efficient air-sac respiration, reduced organs/body mass, and lightweight hollow/honeycombed bones.

close.text: Archaeopteryx and phylogenetic data link birds to theropod dinosaurs, but birds are excluded from Reptilia because flight evolved independently and therefore erases common ancestry.
close.whyWrong: Flight does not erase ancestry; modern systematics nests birds within reptiles/dinosaurs.

close.text: Feathers, air sacs, lightweight bones, and reduced body mass support flight, but birds rely on inefficient tidal lungs rather than the specialized respiratory system highlighted in lecture.
close.whyWrong: Efficient air-sac ventilation is a major flight adaptation.

medium.text: Birds are reptiles because both are ectothermic and have identical scaly bodies with no feathers.
medium.whyWrong: Birds are endothermic and feathered; ancestry is supported by fossils, morphology, and molecular phylogeny.

medium.text: The four flight features are a swim bladder, operculum, lateral line, and cartilaginous skeleton.
medium.whyWrong: Those are fish-related features, not bird flight adaptations.

clear.text: Birds evolved directly from mammals.
clear.whyWrong: They arose within theropod dinosaur reptiles.

clear.text: Hollow/light bones make birds too heavy to fly.
clear.whyWrong: Lightweight skeletal architecture reduces mass while maintaining support.

prompt: What four features distinguish mammals, and what trait does not uniquely distinguish them?
correct: Mammary glands, hair, specialized differentiated teeth, and enlarged skull/jaw-ear modifications distinguish mammals. Endothermy does not uniquely distinguish mammals because birds are also endothermic.
correctWhy: Mammary glands, hair, specialized differentiated teeth, and enlarged skull/jaw-ear modifications distinguish mammals. Endothermy does not uniquely distinguish mammals because birds are also endothermic.

close.text: Mammary glands, hair, specialized teeth, and characteristic skull/jaw-ear modifications distinguish mammals, but endothermy is unique to mammals and absent from birds.
close.whyWrong: Birds are also endothermic, so endothermy is not uniquely mammalian.

close.text: Hair and mammary glands are mammalian traits, but differentiated teeth are absent from mammals and occur only in reptiles.
close.whyWrong: Heterodont/specialized dentition is a key mammalian feature.

medium.text: Mammals are distinguished by feathers, hollow bones, air sacs, and a beak, while endothermy is uniquely mammalian because birds rely on external heat sources.
medium.whyWrong: Those are bird flight-related features, and birds are also endothermic. Mammalian traits include mammary glands, hair, specialized teeth, and skull/jaw-ear modifications.

medium.text: Mammals are identified by gills, a lateral line, a swim bladder, and fin rays; hair is the trait that does not uniquely distinguish them because all vertebrates have it at some stage.
medium.whyWrong: Those are fish traits, and hair is a mammalian feature. Endothermy is the non-unique trait because birds are also endothermic.

clear.text: The four mammalian features are a chitin exoskeleton, six jointed legs, compound eyes, and tracheae; endothermy is not unique because insects are also endothermic vertebrates.
clear.whyWrong: That describes arthropod/insect traits and misclassifies insects. Mammals are characterized by mammary glands, hair, specialized teeth, and skull/jaw-ear modifications; birds also share endothermy.

clear.text: Mammals are defined by scales, a three-chambered heart, external fertilization, and a shell-covered egg laid on land; mammary glands are not unique because reptiles nurse their young with milk.
clear.whyWrong: Those traits do not define mammals, and mammary glands are characteristically mammalian. The trait not unique to mammals is endothermy because birds share it.

prompt: Compare monotremes/prototherians, marsupials/metatherians, and placental/eutherian mammals.
correct: Monotremes lay eggs and lack a placenta. Marsupials are viviparous with a simple short-lived placenta and very underdeveloped newborns that often continue development in a pouch. Eutherians are viviparous with a long-lived complex placenta and prolonged gestation.
correctWhy: Monotremes lay eggs and lack a placenta. Marsupials are viviparous with a simple short-lived placenta and very underdeveloped newborns that often continue development in a pouch. Eutherians are viviparous with a long-lived complex placenta and prolonged gestation.

close.text: Monotremes lay eggs, marsupials give birth to highly underdeveloped young after a short/simple placental connection, and eutherians have a long-lived complex placenta; however, monotremes also have a true placenta and prolonged gestation.
close.whyWrong: Monotremes are egg-laying mammals and do not use a eutherian-style placenta.

close.text: Marsupials and eutherians are both viviparous, but marsupials typically have longer gestation and a more complex placenta than eutherians.
close.whyWrong: Eutherians generally have the longer-lived, more complex placenta and prolonged gestation.

medium.text: Monotremes are reptiles, marsupials are birds, and eutherians are fish.
medium.whyWrong: All three are mammalian reproductive lineages.

medium.text: All three groups reproduce identically by laying shelled eggs.
medium.whyWrong: Only monotremes lay eggs; marsupials and eutherians are viviparous.

clear.text: Marsupials lack mammary glands and therefore are not mammals.
clear.whyWrong: Marsupials are mammals and nurse young.

clear.text: Eutherians have no placenta despite their common name placental mammals.
clear.whyWrong: A complex placenta is a defining reproductive feature of eutherians.
